security_spec.violation_condition: FreeBSD kernel code or bhyve VMM uses the pre-PR#696 IPRIO derivation rules (distinguishing iprio[i]=0 cases as 'higher/lower than machine external interrupt') to compute threshold comparisons when hardware implements the simplified IPRIO-delegated-to-AIA definition, causing xtopi-reported priority to diverge from the kernel's expected masking behavior
security_spec.summary: Delegating IPRIO derivation entirely to AIA breaks hardcoded default-priority assumptions in FreeBSD's interrupt masking logic: if bhyve or the kernel caches old iprio[i]=0 rules, threshold gating may silence critical interrupts or leak masked ones through

findings.finding: IDC_ITHRESHOLD and IDC_TOPI registers are no-ops: guest writes to the interrupt-priority threshold are silently discarded, and reads of TOPI return uninitialized/zeroed data. The VMM APLIC does not implement the AIA priority-threshold masking model at all, meaning a guest OS that writes iprio[i] and expects threshold-based interrupt filtering will observe that all interrupts are delivered regardless of configured priority. This directly corresponds to the spec's xtopi-priority-divergence condition.

CLAIMI always reports priority 0: the priority field is hardcoded to zero in the claimi response regardless of any per-interrupt priority that may have been configured by the guest via sourcecfg or target registers. This means the VMM APLIC cannot represent the AIA simplified-IPRIO model where the hardware (AIA) autonomously derives xtopi from iprio, because the VMM never stores or consults per-irq priority values.

aplic_check_pending only tests enabled && pending; it does not compare interrupt priority against the threshold register (which is itself unimplemented). This means all pending enabled interrupts are treated equally, with no priority-based masking. A guest OS expecting the AIA simplified-IPRIO threshold model will receive interrupts that hardware (or a correct VMM) would have masked.

The hypcsr struct (riscv.h:56-68) and its save/restore paths do not include hviprio1 or hviprio2 CSRs. These AIA-dedicated priority CSRs are neither saved, restored, nor intercepted. If a guest attempts to program per-cause interrupt priorities via hviprio1/hviprio2, the VMM has no visibility and the guest's priority configuration is lost across VM-exit/VM-entry transitions.

The riscvreg.h header defines HVIP_VSSIP/VSTIP/VSEIP bits but does not define hviprio1, hviprio2, or hvictl CSR bit layouts. None of the kernel's CSR inline-assembly macros reference these AIA priority CSRs. This confirms the kernel has no awareness of the simplified-IPRIO-delegated-to-AIA CSR interface, so neither the VMM nor the bare-metal interrupt path can correctly virtualize or configure priority-based masking.
findings.snippet:
#define HVIP_VSSIP (1 << 2)
#define HVIP_VSTIP (1 << 6)
#define HVIP_VSEIP (1 << 10)
/* hviprio1, hviprio2, hvictl: absent */

findings.finding: The bare-metal APLIC driver sets threshold=0 (accept all) and uses a uniform default priority of 1 for all interrupts. It delegates all priority/threshold comparison to the hardware APLIC, which implements the correct AIA IPRIO model. No special-case handling of iprio=0 vs. machine-external-interrupt priority comparisons exists in this driver.

PLIC driver sets threshold to 0 (accept all priorities) on all CPUs. Priority is treated as binary (0=disabled, 1=enabled). The PLIC has no AIA IPRIO concept and is unaffected by the simplified-IPRIO definition change.
